items.stem: By default, how do quantifiers such as + and * behave?

options.text: Greedily, matching as much as possible before backtracking
options.rationale: Correct: default quantifiers are greedy; add ? (for example +?) to make them lazy.

options.text: Lazily, matching as little as possible
options.rationale: Lazy behaviour requires an explicit ?; the default is greedy.
+ and * allow many repetitions, not exactly one.

options.text: They are ignored outside character classes
options.rationale: Quantifiers apply to the preceding token in the pattern.

items.explanation: Correct: default quantifiers are greedy; add ? (for example +?) to make them lazy.

items.stem: Which statements about lookaround assertions are correct? (Select TWO)

options.text: Lookaround is zero-width: it tests a condition without consuming characters
options.rationale: Correct: the matched position does not advance past the lookaround content.

options.text: A negative lookahead (?!...) succeeds only when the pattern does not follow
options.rationale: Correct: (?!...) asserts that what follows does not match.

options.text: Lookahead always consumes the characters it inspects
options.rationale: Lookaround is zero-width and consumes nothing.

options.text: Every regex engine supports variable-length lookbehind
options.rationale: Many engines restrict lookbehind to fixed length; support varies.

items.explanation: Correct: the matched position does not advance past the lookaround content.; Correct: (?!...) asserts that what follows does not match.

items.stem: What is the main risk of a pattern like (a+)+ applied to a long non-matching string?

options.text: Catastrophic backtracking, causing runtime to explode toward exponential
options.rationale: Correct: nested quantifiers create many ways to split the input, so backtracking can blow up.
The pattern compiles; the problem is runtime behaviour.
The danger is slow backtracking, not over-matching.
The issue is CPU time from backtracking, not under-use of memory.
